learn.b: England started its first lasting colony at Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607. In 1620 the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth. Over time there were 13 British colonies along the Atlantic coast.
After a costly war with France, Britain taxed the colonies with laws like the Stamp Act. Colonists had no vote in Parliament, so they said 'no taxation without representation.'
The war began at Lexington and Concord in 1775. Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, adopted in 1776. The British army surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.

qs.q: Which was the first lasting English colony in America?
qs.why: Jamestown, founded in 1607, was the first permanent English colony.

qs.q: What did 'no taxation without representation' protest?
o: Taxes made by Britain without a colonial vote
qs.why: Colonists had no members in Parliament, yet Parliament taxed them.

qs.q: Who was the main writer of the Declaration of Independence?
qs.why: Thomas Jefferson wrote the first draft of the Declaration.

qs.q: Which battles started the Revolutionary War in 1775?
qs.why: The first shots were fired at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.

qs.q: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in 1789.
qs.why: It was adopted in 1776; 1789 is when the new government under the Constitution began.

lab.hint: It is the year of the American Revolution's big declaration.
lab.why: It was adopted on July 4, 1776.

lab.hint: It was named after King James.
lab.why: Jamestown, Virginia, was founded in 1607.

learn.b: The Articles of Confederation gave the national government too little power. In 1787 leaders wrote the Constitution, which made a stronger government with three branches. The Bill of Rights added ten amendments.
In 1803 the US bought the Louisiana Purchase from France, doubling its size. Many Americans believed in Manifest Destiny, the idea that the nation should stretch to the Pacific.
Cotton farming grew after the cotton gin, and it increased slavery in the South. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to the Trail of Tears, when Native Americans were forced from their homelands.

qs.q: How many branches of government does the Constitution create?
qs.why: Legislative, executive, and judicial branches.

qs.q: From which country did the US buy the Louisiana Territory in 1803?
qs.why: Napoleon's France sold the land for about 15 million dollars.

qs.q: What is the Bill of Rights?
o: The first ten amendments to the Constitution
A treaty that ended a war
qs.why: It protects basic freedoms like speech and religion.

qs.q: What was the Trail of Tears?
o: A Gold Rush route to California
Forced removal of Native Americans from the Southeast
qs.why: Cherokee and other nations were forced to move west in the 1830s.

qs.q: The Articles of Confederation created a very strong central government.
qs.why: It was weak, which is why the Constitution replaced it.

pairs: Belief the US should reach the Pacific
Warned Europe to stay out of the Americas

lab.hint: It was a few years after the Revolution ended.
lab.why: The Constitution was signed in 1787.

lab.hint: Thomas Jefferson was president.
lab.why: The Louisiana Purchase was made in 1803.

learn.b: The Erie Canal opened in 1825 and made it cheaper to ship goods from the Great Lakes to New York. Settlers followed the Oregon Trail west. The US also gained Texas in 1845, and after the Mexican-American War (1846-1848) it won California and more land in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

Many Americans wanted to improve society. Some fought against alcohol (temperance), and Horace Mann pushed for public schools. Abolitionists like William Lloyd Garrison, who published The Liberator in 1831, wanted to end slavery.

learn.h: Rights for women and the enslaved
learn.b: In 1848 women met at the Seneca Falls Convention in New York to demand equal rights, including the vote. Harriet Tubman and others helped enslaved people escape north on the Underground Railroad, a secret network of safe houses.

qs.q: Which waterway linked the Hudson River to the Great Lakes?
qs.why: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, made trade between the Midwest and New York cheap and fast.

qs.q: Who published the anti-slavery newspaper The Liberator?
qs.why: Garrison began The Liberator in 1831 to demand an end to slavery.

qs.q: What was the main goal of the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention?
qs.why: Leaders like Elizabeth Cady Stanton demanded women's rights, including the vote.

qs.q: What did the US gain in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)?
qs.why: Mexico gave up a huge area, including California, after the Mexican-American War.

qs.q: The Underground Railroad was a real train that ran under the ground.
qs.why: It was a secret network of people and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape.

pairs: Route settlers used to go west
Person who wanted to end slavery

lab.hint: It opened in the 1820s, five years after the Missouri Compromise.
lab.why: The Erie Canal opened in 1825.

lab.q: Challenge: Which 1848 convention in New York started the women's rights movement? (two words)
lab.hint: It is named after a small town in New York.
lab.why: The Seneca Falls Convention took place in 1848.

lab.hint: Her first name is Harriet.
lab.why: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and guided many others north.

learn.b: The North and South argued over slavery, especially in new western lands. After Abraham Lincoln won the 1860 election, Southern states seceded, or left the Union, and formed the Confederacy.

The war began at Fort Sumter in 1861. Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 declared enslaved people in Confederate states free. The Union won a key battle at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, and the war ended in 1865.

After the war, Reconstruction tried to rebuild the South and bring its states back. The 13th Amendment ended slavery, the 14th gave citizenship to people born in the US, and the 15th protected the right of Black men to vote.

qs.q: Who was the US president during the Civil War?
qs.why: Abraham Lincoln led the Union from 1861 to 1865.

qs.q: What did the 13th Amendment do?
qs.why: It made slavery illegal across the United States.

qs.q: In which state was the Battle of Gettysburg fought?
qs.why: Gettysburg is in Pennsylvania; the Union won there in July 1863.

qs.q: What was the main goal of Reconstruction?
o: Rebuild the South and bring its states back
qs.why: Reconstruction (1865-1877) rebuilt the South and readmitted its states.

qs.q: The Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people free in the Confederate states.
qs.why: It applied to areas in rebellion against the Union.

Northern states loyal to the US
Person who wanted to end slavery

lab.hint: It is a northern state with Philadelphia.
lab.why: Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, was a turning point in 1863.

lab.hint: It is a lucky or unlucky number.
lab.why: The 13th Amendment ended slavery in 1865.

learn.b: After the Civil War, factories and railroads grew fast. The first transcontinental railroad was finished in 1869. Business leaders like Andrew Carnegie (steel) and John D. Rockefeller (Standard Oil) built huge companies, and some became monopolies, controlling a whole industry.

Millions of immigrants arrived, many through Ellis Island in New York Harbor, which opened in 1892. They worked in factories and lived in crowded tenements. In 1882 the Chinese Exclusion Act banned Chinese workers from coming.

Workers formed labor unions to ask for better pay and safer jobs. In the West, the Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of free land to settlers. As settlers moved onto the Plains, Native Americans were pushed onto reservations, and the fighting ended at Wounded Knee in 1890.

qs.q: In which year was the first transcontinental railroad completed?
qs.why: The Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines met at Promontory, Utah, in 1869.

qs.q: What is a monopoly?
o: One company that controls an industry
qs.why: A monopoly has little or no competition, so it can set high prices.

qs.q: Where did many European immigrants enter the US starting in 1892?
qs.why: Ellis Island in New York Harbor was the main immigration station on the East Coast.

qs.q: Which business leader built a huge steel company?
qs.why: Carnegie Steel was among the largest steel producers; Rockefeller was in oil.

qs.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating to the US.
qs.why: It was the first major law to ban a group of immigrants by nationality.

lab.why: Standard Oil controlled most of the US oil refining.

learn.b: Progressives wanted to clean up cities, businesses, and government. Muckrakers were writers who exposed problems. Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle (1906) showed how dirty meatpacking plants were, and Congress passed laws to make food safer. President Theodore Roosevelt broke up trusts, which is called trust-busting.

Reformers changed the Constitution. The 16th Amendment (1913) allowed an income tax and the 17th Amendment (1913) let voters elect senators directly. The 18th Amendment (1919) banned alcohol, and the 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the right to vote.

In the Spanish-American War of 1898, the US took the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico from Spain. Hawaii was annexed that year as well. In 1914 the US opened the Panama Canal, which let ships cross between the Atlantic and Pacific.

qs.q: What did muckrakers do?
o: Wrote stories exposing problems and corruption
qs.why: Muckrakers like Upton Sinclair and Ida Tarbell used writing to push for reform.

qs.q: The Jungle by Upton Sinclair exposed problems in which industry?
qs.why: The book led to food safety laws such as the Meat Inspection Act.

qs.q: Which land did the US take from Spain after the 1898 war?
o: The Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico
qs.why: Cuba became independent, but the US took the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico.

qs.q: Why was the Panama Canal important?
o: It let ships cross between the Atlantic and Pacific
It connected the Great Lakes to the sea
qs.why: The canal saved ships a long trip around South America.

qs.q: The 17th Amendment gave voters the power to elect US senators directly.
qs.why: Before 1913, state legislatures chose senators.

units.title: World War I to the Great Depression

learn.h: The US in World War I
learn.b: Most Americans wanted to stay out of World War I, which began in 1914. In 1917 the US joined the Allies after German submarines sank ships and the Zimmermann Telegram was revealed. President Woodrow Wilson later offered the Fourteen Points as a plan for peace, and the Treaty of Versailles (1919) ended the war with Germany.

The 1920s were a time of jazz, cars, radios, and new styles. The Harlem Renaissance was a flowering of Black art, music, and writing in New York City. Prohibition banned the sale of alcohol, but many people broke the law.

The Dust Bowl was a drought that blew away farm soil on the southern Plains. Millions were out of work. After Franklin D. Roosevelt was elected in 1932, programs like the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) gave people jobs, the FDIC insured bank savings, and the Social Security Act of 1935 helped the elderly.

qs.q: What helped push the US into World War I in 1917?
o: German submarine attacks and the Zimmermann Telegram
qs.why: Germany's attacks on ships and its secret telegram to Mexico angered Americans.

qs.q: What was the Harlem Renaissance?
o: A new way to farm in the Plains
A flowering of Black art, music, and literature
qs.why: Writers like Langston Hughes and musicians like Duke Ellington were part of it.

qs.q: What was the Dust Bowl?
o: Drought and dust storms on the southern Plains
qs.why: Poor farming and drought turned soil into dust, forcing many families to leave.

qs.q: What does the Social Security Act of 1935 provide?
qs.why: It created a system of pensions for retired workers and other aid.

qs.q: Prohibition was a law that banned the sale of alcohol in the US.
qs.why: The 18th Amendment started Prohibition, which lasted until 1933.

learn.b: World War II began in 1939 when Germany invaded Poland. The Axis powers were Germany, Italy, and Japan. The Allies included Britain, the Soviet Union, and later the US. The US helped Britain with weapons through Lend-Lease before it joined the war.

learn.h: Pearl Harbor and the home front
learn.b: On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and the US entered the war. At home, factories made planes and tanks, and women like 'Rosie the Riveter' took war jobs. Under Executive Order 9066 in 1942, Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps.

The US won the Battle of Midway in 1942. On D-Day, June 6, 1944, Allied troops landed in Normandy, France, under General Dwight Eisenhower. Germany surrendered in May 1945. The US built atomic bombs in the Manhattan Project and dropped them on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, and Japan surrendered.

qs.q: Which countries were the main Axis powers?
qs.why: The Axis powers fought against the Allies.

qs.q: What was D-Day?
o: The Allied invasion of Normandy, France
qs.why: On June 6, 1944, Allied troops landed on French beaches.

qs.q: What did Executive Order 9066 lead to?
qs.why: Thousands of Japanese Americans were forced to leave their homes and live in camps.

qs.q: What was the Manhattan Project?
o: A secret program to build the atomic bomb
A plan to rebuild New York
qs.why: Scientists in the US built the first atomic bombs.

qs.q: Germany surrendered before Japan did in 1945.
qs.why: Germany surrendered in May 1945, and Japan in August-September 1945.

units.title: The Cold War and Civil Rights

learn.b: After World War II, the US and the Soviet Union became rivals. The US policy of containment tried to stop the spread of communism. The Marshall Plan gave money to rebuild Europe, NATO was formed in 1949, and in 1948 the Berlin Airlift flew food to West Berlin. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 nearly led to nuclear war.

The US fought in the Korean War (1950-1953) and the Vietnam War. In 1957 the Soviets launched Sputnik, the first satellite, which started the Space Race. President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 because of the Watergate scandal.

In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court said segregated public schools were unconstitutional. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, which led to a boycott. Sit-ins and marches followed, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed unfair voting rules.

qs.q: What was the US policy of containment?
qs.why: The US tried to keep communism from spreading to new countries.

qs.q: What did Brown v. Board of Education (1954) decide?
qs.why: The Court ended legal school segregation, though change took years.

qs.q: In which city did Rosa Parks refuse to give up her bus seat?
qs.why: The Montgomery bus boycott began after her arrest in 1955.

o: Soviet nuclear missiles placed in Cuba
qs.why: The US demanded that the missiles be removed, and the Soviets agreed.

qs.q: The Berlin Airlift delivered food and supplies to West Berlin by plane.

learn.b: After 1877 factories, railroads, and cities grew fast, and millions of immigrants arrived. Reformers pushed for change, and the 19th Amendment in 1920 gave women the right to vote.
The stock market crashed in 1929, starting the Great Depression. President Franklin D. Roosevelt answered with the New Deal. The US joined World War II after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941.

After the war, the US and the Soviet Union competed in the Cold War without fighting each other directly. At home, leaders like Martin Luther King Jr. fought segregation, and the Civil Rights Act passed in 1964.

qs.why: FDR's New Deal programs fought the Great Depression.

qs.why: It was ratified in 1920.

learn.b: In the Paleolithic (Old Stone) Age, people were nomads who moved to follow animals and wild plants. They made stone tools, used fire, and lived in small groups. Objects made by early people, such as tools and cave paintings, are called artifacts.

Around 10,000 BCE, people in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East learned to grow crops and tame animals. This is the Neolithic Revolution. Domestication means changing plants and animals so people can use them, such as wheat and sheep.

Farming made a food surplus, extra food. Because not everyone had to farm, people could become potters, builders, priests, or soldiers. Villages grew into cities along river valleys. In Sumer, people invented cuneiform writing around 3200 BCE.

qs.q: How did Paleolithic people get food?
o: By hunting animals and gathering wild plants
qs.why: They moved around to follow food because they did not farm yet.

qs.q: What was the Neolithic Revolution?
o: The rise of the Roman Empire
The shift from hunting and gathering to farming
qs.why: People began growing crops and raising animals, and settled in villages.

qs.q: Where did farming first develop?
qs.why: The Fertile Crescent in the Middle East had rich soil and wild grains.

qs.q: Why did a food surplus matter?
o: Some people could do jobs other than farming
It stopped the use of tools
qs.why: Extra food freed people to become craftspeople, priests, and leaders.

qs.q: People in the Paleolithic Age lived mostly in large permanent cities.
qs.why: Cities came after farming; Paleolithic people were mostly nomads.

learn.b: The first civilizations grew near rivers. Mesopotamia was between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, and Egypt grew along the Nile. Rivers gave water and rich farmland.
Ancient Greece was made of city-states called poleis. Athens developed an early form of democracy, where citizens voted on laws, while Sparta was known for its army.
Rome began as a republic with a Senate. Julius Caesar's rule and death ended the republic, and Augustus became the first emperor. The Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE.

qs.why: Athenian citizens voted directly on laws.

qs.q: Who was the first emperor of Rome?
qs.why: Augustus became emperor in 27 BCE.

qs.why: Pyramids were royal burial places.

learn.b: The Indus Valley civilization had planned cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro with drains and straight streets. Later, Hinduism grew in India, and Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught Buddhism. Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya Empire supported Buddhism. The Gupta Empire (from 320 CE) was a golden age of math and science, including the idea of zero.

Chinese rulers claimed the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven gave them the right to rule while they ruled well. The philosopher Confucius (born 551 BCE) taught respect for family and good government. A dynasty is a family that rules for many generations.

Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BCE and began the Great Wall. The Han Dynasty began in 206 BCE and traded along the Silk Road. Under the Han, paper was invented and government officials were chosen by exams.

o: The belief that heaven gave rulers the right to rule while they were just
qs.why: If a ruler was cruel, people believed he lost the Mandate.

qs.q: Who unified China in 221 BCE?
qs.why: He became the first emperor of a unified China.

qs.q: Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya Empire supported Buddhism.
qs.why: After a bloody war, Ashoka turned to Buddhism and spread its message of peace.

learn.b: After Rome fell, Europe used feudalism. Kings gave land to lords, lords gave land to vassals, and peasants called serfs worked the land. The Magna Carta of 1215 limited the English king's power.

The Byzantine Empire kept Roman traditions with its capital at Constantinople. Islam spread after Muhammad's Hijra in 622. The Silk Road linked China to the Mediterranean, and Mali's ruler Mansa Musa became famous for his wealth.
The Crusades were Christian military campaigns to control the Holy Land. In the 1340s the Black Death, a plague spread by fleas on rats, killed millions in Europe.

qs.why: Vassals received land in return for loyalty and military service.

qs.q: How was the Black Death spread in Europe?
qs.why: Plague bacteria passed to people through fleas on rats.

qs.q: The Silk Road connected China with what region?
qs.why: Goods like silk and spices traveled between Asia and Europe.

qs.q: What was the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
qs.why: Constantinople is modern Istanbul.

qs.q: The Magna Carta of 1215 limited the power of the English king.
qs.why: It said even the king had to obey the law.

learn.b: Islam began in Mecca with the prophet Muhammad. Muslims follow the Quran, their holy book, and the Five Pillars of Islam: faith, prayer, charity, fasting, and pilgrimage. The Abbasid caliphate (from 750) ruled from Baghdad, where scholars at the House of Wisdom studied math and science.

In West Africa, the empires of Mali and Songhai grew rich from trading gold and salt, and Timbuktu became a center of learning. In Asia, Genghis Khan united the Mongols in 1206 and built the largest land empire in history.

The Maya built cities and used a calendar and the idea of zero. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was built on an island in a lake around 1325. The Inca ruled a huge empire from Cusco in the Andes and kept records with knotted cords called quipus.

qs.q: What are the Five Pillars of Islam?
qs.why: They are faith, prayer, charity, fasting, and pilgrimage.

qs.q: What was the House of Wisdom?
o: A center of learning in Baghdad

European explorers like Columbus crossed the Atlantic, starting the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, and diseases. In 1517 Martin Luther's 95 Theses began the Reformation, which split Western Christianity.

In the Scientific Revolution, Copernicus said the Sun is the center of the solar system. Enlightenment thinkers then stressed reason and individual rights, which inspired revolutions such as the French Revolution.

Enslaved people in Haiti, led by Toussaint Louverture, won independence in 1804. Simon Bolivar led many South American colonies to freedom from Spain.

New machines like James Watt's improved steam engine moved work from homes to factories. Cities grew quickly, which is called urbanization. Factory work was often dangerous, and children worked long hours before reforms.

European countries built colonies in Africa and Asia. At the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, they set rules for dividing Africa without asking Africans. In Japan, the Meiji Restoration (1868) brought quick modernization under the emperor.

learn.b: World War I was fought mostly in trenches on the Western Front, and new weapons like machine guns, poison gas, and tanks caused huge losses. It ended with an armistice on November 11, 1918. In the Treaty of Versailles, Germany had to accept blame and pay reparations, or payments for war damage.

In Russia, Lenin led the Bolsheviks to power in 1917, and later Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union as a dictator. Benito Mussolini became leader of Italy in 1922, using fascism, a system of extreme nationalism under a dictator. Adolf Hitler became Chancellor of Germany in 1933. These were totalitarian governments, which control nearly every part of life.

Britain and France tried appeasement, giving in to Hitler to avoid war, but Germany invaded Poland in 1939. In 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union. The Nazis murdered six million Jews and millions of others in the Holocaust. The war ended in 1945.

learn.b: After World War II, Europe was split by what Winston Churchill called an Iron Curtain, with Communist countries in the East and democracies in the West. NATO (1949) joined Western countries, and the Warsaw Pact (1955) joined Communist ones. Communists under Mao Zedong won in China in 1949. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

Decolonization is when colonies gain independence. India won independence from Britain in 1947 and was divided into India and Pakistan. Ghana became independent in 1957, and many African countries followed. In South Africa, apartheid ended and Nelson Mandela became president in 1994.

Globalization means countries are more connected by trade, travel, technology, and ideas. In 1993 European countries formed the European Union to work together on trade and law. Today the world also faces shared problems like climate change.

World War I began in 1914 after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. World War II ended in 1945, after Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews in the Holocaust. The United Nations was founded in 1945.

learn.b: A government makes laws, keeps order, protects people's rights, and provides services like roads and schools. Thinkers like John Locke said people agree to a social contract: they give some freedom to the government, and in return it protects their life, liberty, and property.

In a monarchy, a king or queen rules; in an absolute monarchy, they have total power. In a dictatorship, one person has unlimited power. An oligarchy is rule by a small group. A theocracy is ruled by religious leaders.
In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves. In a representative democracy, or republic, citizens elect leaders to make laws for them. The United States is a representative democracy.

learn.b: The Constitution is the supreme law of the United States. It begins with 'We the People,' which shows that power comes from the people. This idea is called popular sovereignty.
To stop any one group from getting too strong, power is divided into three branches: legislative, executive, and judicial. Each branch can limit the others, which is called checks and balances.
In federalism, power is shared between the national government and state governments. The Constitution can be changed by amendments. The first ten amendments are the Bill of Rights.

learn.b: At the Constitutional Convention, the Great Compromise created a Congress with two houses: the House (by population) and the Senate (two per state). The Federalist Papers, by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay, argued for approving the Constitution. Critics wanted a Bill of Rights, and the states ratified the Constitution in 1788.

Under federalism, power is divided. Delegated powers belong to the national government, like printing money. Reserved powers belong to the states, like running schools (10th Amendment). Concurrent powers are shared, like collecting taxes. The Supremacy Clause says federal law wins over conflicting state law.
There are 27 amendments. An amendment must be proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and ratified by three-fourths of the states. With 50 states, that means 38 states.

learn.b: Congress is the legislative branch and makes federal laws. It has two parts: the House of Representatives, based on state population, and the Senate, with two senators from each state.

The President leads the executive branch, carries out laws, and is commander in chief of the armed forces. The President can veto a bill, but Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.
The judicial branch includes the Supreme Court. It decides whether laws follow the Constitution, a power called judicial review.

learn.b: The Supreme Court has nine justices, nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, who serve for life during good behavior. Federal and state courts hear cases. A civil case is a dispute between people or groups, and a criminal case is when the government charges someone with a crime. A losing side can appeal, asking a higher court to review the decision.
In Marbury v. Madison (1803), the Court claimed the power of judicial review: deciding whether laws or actions are unconstitutional. Courts also follow precedent, earlier decisions in similar cases.

Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) allowed 'separate but equal', and Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned it for schools. Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) gave the right to a lawyer, Miranda v. Arizona (1966) required police to tell suspects their rights, and Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) protected student speech.

Over time, amendments widened voting rights. The 19th gave women the vote and the 26th set the voting age at 18.
Citizens have duties such as obeying laws, paying taxes, and serving on a jury when called. People born elsewhere can become citizens through naturalization.

An interest group is a group of people with a shared goal who try to influence government. Lobbying means trying to persuade lawmakers. A political action committee (PAC) raises money to support candidates.

The press is a watchdog that reports on government, protected by the First Amendment. Media bias is slanted coverage. Polls ask a sample of people what they think. Smart citizens check sources and compare reports.

learn.b: Governments get revenue from taxes: income tax on earnings, sales tax on purchases, and property tax on land and buildings. The federal budget pays for things like defense, Social Security, and Medicare. A deficit happens when government spends more than it takes in during a year.

Foreign policy is how a country deals with other countries. Diplomacy means peaceful talks. Ambassadors represent their country abroad, and the Secretary of State leads the State Department. A tariff is a tax on imported goods, and a sanction is a penalty used to pressure a country.

The President negotiates treaties, but the Senate must approve them by a two-thirds vote. The US belongs to groups like the United Nations, which helps countries work on peace, and NATO, a military alliance.

learn.b: Latitude lines run east-west and measure distance north or south of the equator. Longitude lines run north-south and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian, which passes through Greenwich, England.
The equator splits Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. There are seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.
A legend explains the symbols on a map. A scale shows how map distance matches real distance. The Pacific is the largest ocean.

qs.q: Which lines measure distance north or south of the equator?
qs.why: Latitude measures north-south position.

qs.q: The prime meridian passes through which place?
qs.why: Greenwich is at 0 degrees longitude.

qs.q: How many continents are there?
qs.why: The common model counts seven continents.

qs.q: What does the equator divide Earth into?
qs.why: The equator is 0 degrees latitude.

qs.q: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean on Earth.
qs.why: It covers about one third of Earth's surface.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Distance north or south of equator
Distance east or west of prime meridian

lab.hint: They are parallel to the equator.

lab.q: Challenge: How many continents are there? (a number)
lab.hint: It is more than five and less than eight.
lab.why: There are seven continents.

lab.q: Challenge: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?

learn.b: Earth's outer shell is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates that move slowly. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift, the idea that continents were once joined in one supercontinent called Pangaea. Plates meet at three kinds of boundaries.

At a divergent boundary, plates move apart. At a convergent boundary, plates collide, which can build mountains like the Himalayas. At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other, like along the San Andreas Fault in California.

Earthquakes happen when plates suddenly slip along faults, and a seismograph measures them. Many volcanoes and quakes occur around the Pacific Ocean in the Ring of Fire. Weathering breaks rock down, erosion carries it away, and deposition drops it to build new land.

qs.q: Who proposed the idea of continental drift?
qs.why: Wegener noticed the continents fit together like puzzle pieces.

qs.q: What do we call plates sliding past each other?
qs.why: The San Andreas Fault is a famous example.

qs.q: Where is the Ring of Fire?
o: Around the edge of the Pacific Ocean
qs.why: Many volcanoes and earthquakes happen there.

qs.q: What tool measures earthquakes?
qs.why: A seismograph records ground shaking.

qs.q: The Himalayas formed where two plates collided.
qs.why: The Indian Plate pushed into the Eurasian Plate.

Put the steps of landform change in order

lab.q: Challenge: Wegener's idea that continents move is called continental ___.
lab.hint: It means to move slowly.
lab.why: Wegener called it continental drift.

lab.q: Challenge: The ancient supercontinent was called ___.
lab.hint: The name means 'all lands'.
lab.why: Pangaea broke apart over millions of years.

lab.q: Challenge: The belt of volcanoes around the Pacific is called the Ring of ___.
lab.hint: It is hot.
lab.why: The Ring of Fire has many volcanoes and quakes.

learn.b: A peninsula is land surrounded by water on three sides. A plateau is high, flat land. A delta forms where a river meets the sea. An archipelago is a group of islands. Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level.
Weather is what the air is like today. Climate is the usual weather pattern over many years. Places near the equator are usually warm, and places near the poles are cold.
A biome is a large natural region, such as rainforest, desert, or tundra. Tundra has permanently frozen ground. Earth has four layers: crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.

qs.q: Which is the highest mountain above sea level?
qs.why: Everest is about 8,849 meters high.

qs.q: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
qs.why: The Sahara in Africa is the largest hot desert.

qs.q: What is climate?
o: The usual weather pattern over many years
qs.why: Climate is long-term; weather is short-term.

qs.q: Which biome has permanently frozen ground?
qs.why: Tundra has permafrost beneath the surface.

qs.q: Tropical rainforests receive very little rainfall.
qs.why: Rainforests are among the wettest places on Earth.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Land with water on three sides
Land formed at a river's mouth

lab.hint: It is in the Himalayas.
lab.why: Mount Everest is about 8,849 meters high.

lab.q: Challenge: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
lab.hint: It covers much of North Africa.
lab.why: The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

lab.q: Challenge: Land formed at a river's mouth from deposited sediment is a ___.
lab.hint: It is also a Greek letter.

learn.b: Water moves in a cycle. Evaporation turns liquid water into vapor, condensation turns vapor into droplets that form clouds, precipitation brings rain or snow, and collection gathers water in oceans, lakes, and rivers.

Weather is the short-term condition of the air, while climate is the long-term pattern. Ocean currents like the Gulf Stream carry warm water and warm Western Europe. A hurricane is called a typhoon in the western Pacific. A monsoon is a seasonal wind that brings heavy rain, especially in South Asia.

A biome is a large region with similar climate, plants, and animals. Examples are desert, tropical rainforest, savanna (tropical grassland with scattered trees), and taiga (a cold forest of evergreen trees in northern Russia and Canada). Higher elevation usually means cooler temperatures.

qs.q: What is a typhoon?
o: A hurricane in the western Pacific
qs.why: The same kind of storm has different names in different oceans.

qs.q: What does the Gulf Stream do?
o: Carries warm water that warms Western Europe
qs.why: It makes Western Europe warmer than other places at similar latitudes.

qs.q: What is a monsoon?
o: A seasonal wind that brings heavy rain
qs.why: South Asia gets much of its rain from the summer monsoon.

qs.q: What is taiga?
o: A cold forest of evergreen trees
qs.why: It stretches across northern Canada, Russia, and Scandinavia.

qs.q: Weather describes the long-term pattern of conditions in a region.
qs.why: That is climate; weather is short-term.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the water cycle in order

lab.hint: This forms clouds.
lab.why: Condensation makes clouds.

lab.q: Challenge: A hurricane in the western Pacific is called a ___.
lab.hint: It starts with T.
lab.why: The same storm is a hurricane, typhoon, or cyclone by region.

lab.q: Challenge: The tropical grassland biome with scattered trees, found in Africa, is the ___.
lab.hint: Lions live here.
lab.why: Savannas have grass and scattered trees.

learn.b: India and China have the largest populations in the world. Population density means how many people live in a certain area. Many people now live in cities, a trend called urbanization.

Migration is moving from one place to live in another. Push factors, like war or famine, drive people away. Pull factors, like jobs or safety, attract them. An emigrant leaves a country and an immigrant enters one.

Culture means the customs, beliefs, and language a group shares. Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers of any language. A capital city is the seat of government and is not always the largest city.

qs.q: Which two countries have the largest populations?
qs.why: India and China each have more than 1.4 billion people.

qs.q: What is urbanization?
o: Growth of cities as more people live there
qs.why: Urbanization means a rising share of people living in cities.

qs.q: Which is an example of a push factor in migration?
qs.why: Push factors drive people away from their home.

qs.q: Which language has the most native speakers?
qs.why: Mandarin has more native speakers than any other language.

qs.q: A country's capital city is always its largest city.
qs.why: For example, Canberra is Australia's capital, but Sydney is larger.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these settlements from smallest to largest

lab.hint: It starts with 'im'.
lab.why: An immigrant moves into a new country.

lab.q: Challenge: Which language has the most native speakers?
lab.hint: It is spoken in China.
lab.why: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers.

lab.q: Challenge: The growth of cities as more people live there is called ___.
lab.hint: It starts with 'urban'.
lab.why: Urbanization is the growth of cities.

learn.b: Demography is the study of populations. A census is an official count of people. The birth rate and death rate are usually measured per 1,000 people. Natural increase equals the birth rate minus the death rate. Life expectancy is the average number of years a person is expected to live.

Population density is people per unit of area: population divided by area. A country can be crowded even if it is small. A population pyramid shows ages and sexes. A wide base means many young people, as in fast-growing countries.

Pull factors attract people to a place, like jobs or safety. People moving within a country is internal migration. Many countries go through stages: first both birth and death rates are high, then death rates fall, then birth rates fall, and both end up low.

qs.q: What is natural increase?
qs.why: If births are higher than deaths, the population grows naturally.

qs.q: What does a wide base on a population pyramid show?
qs.why: The bottom of the pyramid shows the youngest ages.

qs.q: Which is a pull factor?
qs.why: Pull factors attract people to a new place.

qs.q: What does life expectancy measure?
o: Average years a person is expected to live
qs.why: It is a common measure of health and well-being.

qs.q: A country with a small area always has a small population density.
qs.why: Density depends on both people and area; a small country with many people is dense.

lab.hint: Subtract the death rate from the birth rate.

lab.hint: The US holds one every ten years.
lab.why: A census counts the population.

learn.b: The primary sector gets raw materials, such as farming and mining. The secondary sector makes goods in factories. The tertiary sector provides services, such as teaching and shops. GDP, or Gross Domestic Product, measures the value of all goods and services a country makes in a year.

Goods sold to other countries are exports, and goods bought from other countries are imports. A tariff is a tax on imports. Developed countries usually have higher incomes and more services than developing countries.

A border separates countries. Natural boundaries follow features like rivers and mountains, while others are straight lines drawn by people. The United Nations has 193 member countries, and the European Union is a group of European countries that share trade rules.

qs.q: Mining belongs to which sector?
qs.why: It takes raw materials from the earth.

qs.q: What does GDP measure?
o: The value of goods and services a country produces
qs.why: It is a common way to measure a country's economy.

qs.q: What are exports?
qs.why: Imports are goods bought from other countries.

qs.q: Which is a natural boundary?
o: A straight line on a map
qs.why: Rivers and mountains often mark borders.

qs.q: A tariff is a tax on imported goods.
qs.why: Tariffs make imports more expensive.

lab.hint: The prefix 'ex' means out.

learn.b: Renewable resources, like solar, wind, and water power, can be replaced naturally. Nonrenewable resources, like coal, oil, and natural gas, are fossil fuels that take millions of years to form.
When fossil fuels burn, they release carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the air. More greenhouse gases make Earth warmer, which raises sea levels as ice melts.

Deforestation is the clearing of forests, such as in the Amazon rainforest, the world's largest rainforest. Desertification is fertile land turning into desert. Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming future generations, and conservation means protecting resources.

qs.q: Which is a renewable energy source?
qs.why: Wind keeps blowing, so it can be used again and again.

qs.q: Which gas from burning fossil fuels traps heat?
qs.why: It is the main greenhouse gas from human activity.

qs.q: What is deforestation?
qs.why: Forests are cut for farms, wood, and cities.

qs.q: What is sustainability?
o: Meeting today's needs without harming the future
Using resources as fast as possible

qs.q: Coal, oil, and natural gas are renewable resources.

learn.b: Russia is the largest country by area, followed by Canada and China. The Nile flows through Egypt and the Amazon flows through Brazil.
Every country has a capital. Tokyo is the capital of Japan, Cairo of Egypt, Ottawa of Canada, Nairobi of Kenya, and Brasilia of Brazil.

Africa has the most countries of any continent. Australia is both a country and a continent. Oslo is far north, Rome is in the middle latitudes, Nairobi is near the equator, and Cape Town is in the far south.

qs.q: Which country is the largest by area?
qs.why: Russia covers more than 17 million square kilometers.

units.title: Africa, Asia, and the Middle East

learn.b: The Sahara is in North Africa and the Nile flows north to the Mediterranean. Mount Kilimanjaro, in Tanzania, is Africa's highest mountain, and the Great Rift Valley is a long valley in East Africa.

The Yangtze is Asia's longest river, in China, and the Ganges is a sacred river in India. The Gobi is a desert in Mongolia and China. Japan and Indonesia are archipelagos, groups of islands. Capitals include Beijing (China), New Delhi (India), and Tokyo (Japan).
The Middle East has deserts and rich oil reserves around the Persian Gulf. Riyadh is the capital of Saudi Arabia. The Dead Sea, between Israel and Jordan, is the lowest point on land.

qs.why: It is in Tanzania and is about 5,895 meters high.

qs.q: Which is the longest river in Asia?
qs.why: It flows across China to the East China Sea.

qs.why: Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, and others hold huge oil reserves.

qs.why: It lies about 430 meters below sea level.

qs.why: It is in Tanzania, near the Kenyan border.
